p: Little is known of how the work came into being. Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, of the 1st century BCE, calls it Master Zuo's Spring and Autumn Annals and says that Zuo compiled it from the scribal records of Confucius to preserve the true teachings. The identification of this Zuo with the Zuo Qiuming praised in the Analects rests on no specific evidence and was challenged as early as the 8th century. Excavated manuscripts and analysis of its language suggest that its composition was largely complete by 300 BCE.

In the early 19th century Liu Fenglu argued that the text was not originally a commentary on the Annals, a view now generally accepted. Kang Youwei went further and held that the Han scholar Liu Xin had forged it; that theory is now considered discredited. The present arrangement, in which each entry of the Annals is followed by the matching narrative, was made by Du Yu in the 3rd century CE.

The work has 30 chapters and tells its events from the perspective of the State of Lu. Each year opens with the terse entry of the Annals, followed by narratives that are often long and detailed: battles, assassinations, intrigue, oppression and uprisings, ghosts and portents. Because the order is strictly chronological, connected episodes may be separated by the events of intervening years. Its account of the Battle of Chengpu in 632 BCE, in which the State of Jin under Chong'er defeated the State of Chu, is typical in giving more space to preparations, omens and the division of spoils than to the fighting.

The narration stays in the third person and conveys its lessons through speech and action: the haughty and wicked generally bring disaster on themselves, and ritual propriety governs all conduct, including war, though the good are also shown suffering senseless violence. Many anecdotes end with a brief verdict attributed to Confucius or to an unnamed gentleman; these were added later by Confucian scholars.

The work was canonised as one of the Chinese classics in the 1st century CE and remained a cornerstone of education in China, Japan and Korea until modern times. It is the source of more chengyu, or set idioms, than any other work, and the Qing anthology Guwen Guanzhi took 34 passages from it, more than from any other source. The oldest surviving manuscripts are six fragments found among the Dunhuang manuscripts by Paul Pelliot, dating from the 3rd to the 7th century.

notes: The article gives the Spring and Autumn period as 771-476 BCE and the work's coverage as 722-468 BCE, and once calls the period covered '400-year'; I repeated none of these beyond what the entry has.
Karlgren's dating 'between 468 and 300 BC' left out for space; the entry's fourth-century date agrees with the article's 'most scholars'.
